name: Ishvara Temple, Arasikere
significance: A Hoysala-period Shiva temple raised around 1220 under Narasimha II, notable for an unusually complex plan in which a sixteen-pointed star-shaped hall is joined to a five-storeyed vimana. Its outer walls carry roughly 120 relief panels drawing on Shaiva, Vaishnava, Shakta and Vedic subject matter.

name: Amrutesvara Temple, Amruthapura
significance: Built in 1196 during the reign of the Hoysala king Veera Ballala II by his commander Amrutheshwara Dandanayaka, this medium-sized ekakuta shrine is valued for its wide open hall and finely worked Hoysala sculpture.
story: The tower over the vestibule carries the Hoysala emblem of Sala fighting a lion, the mythical founding episode from which the dynasty took its name.

name: Veera Narayana Temple, Belavadi
deity: Vishnu as Veeranarayana, with Yoga-Narasimha and Venugopala
significance: A three-shrined Hoysala temple completed around 1200 under Veera Ballala II, with the central sanctum holding Veeranarayana and flanking shrines for Yoga-Narasimha and Venugopala. Its stellate plan and Vesara superstructures make it one of the larger surviving Hoysala trikuta layouts.
story: Local tradition traces the village to the Mahabharata, holding that the Pandava prince Bhima killed the demon Bakasura here and delivered the settlement.

name: Doddabasappa Temple
significance: A twelfth-century Shiva temple of the Western Chalukya period, distinguished by an unusually elaborate twenty-four-pointed star-shaped plan carried without interruption through a seven-tiered dravida superstructure.

name: Trikuteshwara Temple, Gadag
deity: Shiva (three lingas on a single stone)
significance: A Shiva temple of the Kalyani Chalukya era, named for the three lingas set on one stone in its sanctum, and known for its lathe-turned ornate pillars and pierced stone screens. The complex also contains a much-visited shrine to Saraswati.

name: Mahadeva Temple, Itagi
significance: Raised around 1112 by Mahadeva, a commander under the Western Chalukya emperor Vikramaditya VI, this temple pairs dravida wall articulation with a nagara superstructure and is ringed by thirteen subsidiary linga shrines. A contemporary inscription calls it Devalaya Chakravarti, emperor among temples.

name: Kalleshvara Temple, Bagali
deity: Shiva, with shrines to Surya and Narasimha
builtDisplay: 10th c. (Rashtrakuta, completed c. 987 under Tailapa II)
significance: A rare temple whose fabric spans two Kannada dynasties: a late Rashtrakuta vimana and closed hall of the mid-tenth century, fronted by an open hall added around 987 under the founding Western Chalukya king Tailapa II. Its shrines to Surya and Narasimha sit alongside the main Shiva sanctum.

name: Yellamma Temple, Saundatti
significance: A hilltop shrine to the goddess Yellamma, identified with Renuka and revered as a deity of fertility, drawing very large pilgrim gatherings from Karnataka and neighbouring states. The present structure was built in 1514 by Bomappa Nayaka of Raybag on a site that had held a temple since the Rashtrakuta and later Chalukya centuries.
story: The katha tells how Renuka, wife of the sage Jamadagni, broke her vow of chastity and was beheaded by her son Parashurama at his father's command, only to be restored to life by the sage; some versions say she was revived with another woman's head, which is why she is also called Yellamma.

name: Saavira Kambada Basadi (Thousand Pillar Temple), Moodabidri
significance: The principal Jain basadi of Moodabidri, begun in 1430 by the local chieftain Devaraya Wodeyar and named for the many carved pillars of its sequence of halls. Its sanctum holds an eight-foot panchadhatu image of the Tirthankara Chandraprabha.

name: Namdroling Monastery
significance: The largest teaching centre of the Nyingma school of Tibetan Buddhism outside Tibet, founded in 1963 at the Bylakuppe Tibetan settlement by Penor Rinpoche, eleventh throneholder of the Palyul lineage. It remains the seat of that lineage, now led by its twelfth throneholder, Karma Kuchen.

name: Attukal Bhagavathy Temple
deity: Bhagavathy, identified with Bhadrakali and with Kannagi
significance: A goddess temple close to the centre of Thiruvananthapuram whose deity is understood both as Bhadrakali and as Kannagi, the heroine of the Tamil epic Cilappatikaram. It is best known for the Attukal Pongala, a mass offering cooked by women that draws enormous crowds each year.
story: Tradition holds that the goddess appeared as a radiant girl to the head of the Mulluveettil family at the Killi river, vanished, and then came to him in a dream directing him to consecrate her in a sacred grove at a spot she marked with three lines.

name: Chottanikkara Temple
significance: One of Kerala's most visited goddess temples, where the same deity is worshipped in three aspects through the day: Saraswati in the morning, Lakshmi at noon and Durga in the evening. It has a long reputation as a place of healing for the mentally distressed.
story: A tribal named Kannappan who sacrificed buffaloes to the goddess found a divine calf embodying Vishnu and Lakshmi, and after his daughter's death was read as punishment for his cruelty, his altar became the sacred shrine.

name: Vaikom Mahadeva Temple
significance: A major Shiva temple of central Kerala whose lingam is venerated as Vaikathappan, set in a large walled compound with an unusual oval sanctum that reads as circular from outside.
story: The demon Khara received three lingams from Shiva at Chidambaram, and on his southward journey one of them would not be moved again, fixing the temple's site, where the sage Vyaghrapada later became its custodian.

name: Ettumanoor Mahadevar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in Kottayam district rebuilt in its present form in 1542, celebrated for its murals and for the seven and a half golden elephants displayed during its annual festival.
story: Temple tradition holds that the Pandavas and the sage Vyasa worshipped here.

name: Kadampuzha Devi Temple
deity: Parvati as a huntress, worshipped in a pit rather than as an image
significance: An unusual Kerala goddess shrine with no installed image: the deity is worshipped in a pit, in her form as a huntress. It is known for the offering of muttarukkal, made by devotees seeking the removal of obstacles.
story: During the Pandavas' exile Arjuna performed severe penance here to obtain the Pashupatastra, and Shiva, disguised as a hunter alongside Parvati, tested his pride before granting it.

name: Kodungallur Sree Kurumba Bhagavathy Temple
significance: One of the oldest and most important Bhadrakali temples in Kerala and a principal centre of the state's goddess worship, best known for the Bharani festival. Its date of foundation is not established, though tradition ties it to the Sangam age.
story: It is told that after Parashurama raised Kerala from the sea the demon Darikan terrorised the land until Bhadrakali sprang from Shiva's three eyes and destroyed him; another tradition identifies the goddess here with Kannaki of the Tamil epic.

name: Mannarasala Sree Nagaraja Temple
significance: The foremost serpent shrine of Kerala, set in a wooded grove filled with thousands of votive serpent images and unusual in being led by a priestess of the resident family.
story: Parashurama is said to have installed Nagaraja here so that the serpents would sweeten the salt-poisoned soil of newly raised Kerala and spare its people.

name: Ambalappuzha Sree Krishna Swamy Temple
deity: Krishna, shown as Parthasarathy with whip and conch
significance: A Krishna temple in Alappuzha district believed to have been built in the fifteenth century by the Chembakasserry ruler Pooradam Thirunal Devanarayanan Thampuran, where the deity is worshipped in the charioteer form of Parthasarathy. It is famous throughout Kerala for its daily palpayasam offering.
story: A sage who was Krishna in disguise beat the local king at chess and claimed rice doubled on each square of the board, a debt no granary could settle, which is why the temple has served payasam to devotees ever since.

name: Chettikulangara Devi Temple
significance: A large Bhadrakali temple in Alappuzha district, reckoned to be around twelve hundred years old, with its present sreekovil dating to about 1540. It is best known for Kettukazhcha, in which the surrounding villages bring towering decorated effigies and chariots to the temple ground.
story: A boatman is said to have ferried a mysterious old woman to Chettikulangara who then vanished, and the people took this as the goddess herself arriving to claim the place for her temple.

name: Parassinikadavu Sree Muthappan Temple
deity: Sree Muthappan, a manifestation of Shiva
significance: A shrine on the Valapattanam river where worship is conducted not through image ritual but through the theyyam performances Thiruvappan and Vellattam, enacted daily. It is unusual among Kerala temples in being open to all castes and communities.
story: A divine boy who appeared as Shiva in the guise of a hunter turned the toddy-tapper Chantan to stone in a quarrel over palm toddy, and after propitiatory rites was honoured as Muthappan and worshipped as a deity.

name: Rajarajeshwara Temple, Taliparamba
significance: A leading Shiva temple of north Kerala, rebuilt into its present form in the early eleventh century after earlier work by the Mushika or Kolathiri rulers, with a square sanctum under a two-tiered pyramidal roof. It was attacked and partly destroyed by Mysorean forces in the late eighteenth century before being repaired.
story: The sage Maandhata is said to have been given a Shiva linga to install where no cremation ground lay, finally setting it at Taliparamba, after which the linga repeatedly vanished and reappeared to later devotees.

name: Thirunelli Temple
significance: A Vishnu temple set among the Brahmagiri hills of Wayanad, reached through forest and long resorted to for ancestral rites performed at the nearby Papanasini stream.
story: Brahma is said to have found an image of Vishnu inside an amla tree at this spot and recognised the place as the god's own heavenly abode.

name: Lokanarkavu Temple
significance: A Durga temple near Vatakara in Kozhikode district, held by its records to be about fifteen hundred years old, and closely bound to the martial culture of northern Malabar.
story: The temple is inseparable from the ballads of the warrior Thacholi Othenan, and practitioners of Kalaripayattu still seek the goddess's blessing here before their first public performance.

name: Sree Poornathrayeesa Temple
significance: The chief temple of Tripunithura and long the tutelary shrine of the Cochin royal family, where Vishnu is worshipped as Poornathrayeesa in the Santhana Gopala form. The present structure was raised after a fire destroyed the earlier building around 1920.
story: It is told that Vishnu gave the image of Poornathrayeesa to Arjuna after restoring to life the ten lost children of a Brahmin, and the sanctum was built in the shape of a chariot to mark that event.

name: Ernakulam Shiva Temple
deity: Shiva in the Gowrisankara form, the lingam held to be swayambhu
significance: The principal Shiva temple of Ernakulam city, from which the place takes its name, referred to in Sangam literature as existing under the Cheras. Its present buildings were put up between 1843 and 1846 under the patronage of Sankara Warrier of Edakkunni.
story: The Mahabharata episode attached to the site tells of Arjuna's severe penance to Shiva, who came disguised as a tribal hunter before granting him the Pashupata weapon.

name: Kaviyoor Mahadevar Temple
deity: Shiva with Parvati, worshipped as Thrikkaviyoorappan
significance: One of the older Shiva temples of central Travancore, its present sanctum dated to the tenth century and carrying two inscriptions of AD 951-952. The Hanuman shrine within the complex is as widely visited as the main sanctum.
story: Rama is said to have installed the Shiva image here on his return from Lanka, and when Hanuman could not replace it with a lingam fetched from the Himalayas the ground rose into a hillock, making Kaviyoor his permanent abode.

name: Oachira Temple (Parabrahma Temple)
significance: An ancient temple in Kollam district dedicated to Parabrahma and remarkable for having neither an image nor a sanctum: worship is offered in the open, under a stand of carefully preserved trees.

name: Janardanaswamy Temple, Varkala
significance: A cliff-top Vishnu temple above the Varkala beach, whose restoration is credited to a Pandya king around the first century BC with further renovation during the reign of Umayamma Rani in 1677-84. Its circular sanctum under a conical copper dome is characteristic of Kerala building.
story: Brahma is said to have cursed the devas to be born as mortals, and they performed penance at Varkala, the place where the sage Narada's cloth fell, building a Vishnu temple there to free themselves.

name: Kamakshi Amman Temple
deity: Kamakshi, an aspect of Adi Shakti
builtDisplay: attributed to the 5th-8th c. (Pallava), with later work
significance: The principal goddess temple of Kanchipuram and one of the foremost centres of Shakta worship in the south, where Kamakshi is seated in padmasana rather than standing. Its origins have been variously placed with the Pallavas between the fifth and eighth centuries and with later Chola-period work.
story: It is told that the goddess Tripura Sundari destroyed the demon Bhandasura and then settled at Kanchipuram; another account says a golden image of Kamakshi was brought here in 1783 after the collapse of Vijayanagara.

name: Samayapuram Mariamman Temple
deity: Samayapuram Mariamman, a form of Adi Parashakti
significance: One of the wealthiest and busiest Mariamman temples in Tamil Nadu, north of Tiruchirappalli, whose present structure was raised in the early eighteenth century by Vijayaraya Chakravarti II. Its deity is sought above all for relief from disease.
story: Tradition says the image once stood at Srirangam and was removed after it was blamed for the presiding deity's illness, then found by passers-by who raised a shrine, the Kannanur Mariamman temple, which grew into the present one.

name: Swaminathaswamy Temple, Swamimalai
significance: The fourth of the six war-camp abodes of Murugan, built on a sixty-foot mound reached by a long stair, with three gopurams and three enclosures and shrines to Sundareswarar and Meenakshi at the foot of the hill.
story: Here the child Murugan is said to have expounded the meaning of the syllable Om to his father Shiva, and so earned the name Swaminatha, teacher of the lord.

name: Subramaniya Swamy Temple, Tiruttani
significance: The fifth of Murugan's six principal abodes, standing on a hill approached by a flight of stone steps and among the most visited pilgrimage temples of northern Tamil Nadu.
story: After destroying the demon Surapadman, Murugan is said to have come to Tiruttani to let his anger subside, and it was here that he married Valli.

name: Pazhamudircholai Murugan Temple
significance: The last of the six war-camp abodes of Murugan, set in dense hill forest north of Madurai, with subsidiary shrines to Ganesha and to Murugan's consorts Valli and Deivanai.
story: The Kanda Puranam relates that Murugan withdrew as a hermit after the fruit of knowledge was awarded to his brother Ganesha, and that when the poet Avvaiyar came to him he shook a naaval tree to offer her its fruit, giving the place its name.

name: Nagaraja Temple, Nagercoil
significance: The serpent temple that gives Nagercoil its name, with a sanctum for the five-headed Nagaraja and further shrines to Ananthakrishna with Rukmini and Satyabhama, and to Shiva. Sixteenth-century inscriptions describe it as a Jain temple, and its pillar carving resembles work of the ninth to twelfth centuries.
story: A Nambudiri Brahmin returning from a Pandyan king's court is said to have rediscovered a Naga image here and begun its worship, later installing Vishnu and Shiva after a vision.

name: Mahamaham Tank
deity: Shiva; focus of the Mahamaham festival
significance: The great bathing tank at the centre of Kumbakonam, dating at least to the sixteenth century, whose sixteen surrounding mandapas and stone ghats were built by Govinda Dikshitar, minister to the Thanjavur Nayak ruler Ragunatha. Its Mahamaham festival, held once every twelve years, is regarded as the southern counterpart of the Kumbh Mela.
story: It is told that Shiva gathered the seeds of all creation into a cosmic pot before the great flood, and when the pot broke its contents formed this tank, to which the nine river goddesses of India come during the festival to renew their waters.

name: Oppiliappan Temple
deity: Vishnu as Oppiliappan, with Lakshmi as Bhudevi
significance: A Divya Desam near Kumbakonam built in the late eighth century by the medieval Cholas and enlarged by the Thanjavur Nayaks in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. It is distinctive for offering all its food to the deity without salt.
story: The sage Markandeya is said to have performed a thousand years of penance to gain Lakshmi as his daughter; she appeared as an infant beneath a tulasi plant, and Vishnu married her on the promise that the food he received would never be salted.
